newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers seek to free heating aid for poor.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers seek to free heating aid for poor.

text.p: Members of Congress asked President Clinton Wednesday to release $420 million in emergency aid to help poor families pay their heating bills during the cold winter months.

The 149 lawmakers, led by Vermont Independent Representative Bernard Sanders, said in a letter to the president that release of the funds was critical due to rising fuel costs that are making it impossible for some low-income families to pay heating bills.
"In the United States of America, low-income senior citizens and children should not be forced to go cold in the winter," the letter said.

The lawmakers want the president to open a special contingency fund under the government's Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Programme. LIHEAP provides money to states to help poor people pay heating or air conditioning bills.
Clinton, who can tap into the fund at his discretion, released $180 million in emergency heating money last winter.
The president Wednesday released $5 million in programme funds to help residents of North and South Dakota deal with an unusually harsh winter.
North Dakota will receive nearly $2.8 million and South Dakota an additional $2.2 million. Last week, Clinton declared both states federal disaster areas because of unusually harsh winter storms.
The lawmakers, including 30 Republicans, said retail heating oil prices in the East and Midwest had been 23 percent higher than last year and propane prices had risen 48 percent.
Funding under the assistance programme is below last year, meaning the ability of poor families to pay heating bills has effectively been cut by 30-55 percent this winter, they said.
While many states bar public utilities from cutting off service for nonpayment during the winter, families that use oil or propane heat do not have the same protections.
The LIHEAP programme served an estimated 5.2 million households last year, 68 percent of those households with incomes of less than $8,000.
